title: Detection of Develop Capabilities
summary: This detection strategy covers the resource development phase of developing capabilities, where an adversary writes or modifies its own tooling, exploits, or payloads instead of buying them. It matters because in house development produces artifacts that are unique to the campaign, such as private source repositories, unsigned builds, and test infrastructure, and those artifacts can be caught before the payload reaches production. The telemetry that makes it possible is source control and code review audit logs, build server records, certificate creation events, and cloud or domain registration activity used to host test infrastructure. The main failure mode is that legitimate developers do the same things every day, so the rule must key on who is building, on which host, and whether the resulting artifact is signed or deployed through a normal release process.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that a person is writing or modifying attack code. Developing a capability means building a tool or program that will be used in an intrusion. The rule watches code repositories, build servers, and certificate creation. It also watches for test systems that appear without a business reason.
beginner.whyItMatters: Custom code is harder to spot, because no known signature matches it. It often starts on a normal workstation with a normal developer account. The build step leaves records that a purchased tool would not leave. Catching the build lets you stop the code before it is used.
howItWorks: The source control system logs each commit, with the author, the branch, and the files changed.
The build server records each job, the triggering account, and the produced artifact.
Certificate creation logs show when a new signing certificate is made for that artifact.
Cloud and hosting logs show test systems that support the new code.
The SIEM links the repository activity to the build, the signing, and the hosting.
An unusual author committing offensive looking code, then building and signing it, raises an alert.
beginner.example: Picture a night watchman who also checks the workshop sign out book. A worker takes metal stock, uses the cutting bench, and books the paint booth after hours. There is no job ticket for the work, so the watchman walks over. Each record is normal by itself. Together they tell a story the watchman can report.
takeaways: Development leaves a chain of records across repository, build, and signing systems.
The strongest signal is a change in who is building, not what the code contains.
Legitimate developers dominate the data, so baselines and scoping are essential.

objectives: Explain what capability development looks like inside an organization.
Identify repository, build, signing and hosting records used for detection.
Write a rule that flags unusual build or commit behaviour.
Describe how to correlate a commit with a later unsigned deployment.
Discuss the risk of over blocking legitimate engineering work.
dataSources: Source control audit logs recording commit author, repository, branch, file paths and review approval state
Build server job logs recording triggering account, build definition, artifact name and artifact hash
Internal certificate authority logs recording issuance of new code signing certificates and templates
Endpoint process creation records for compilers, packers and script build tools on non engineering hosts
logic: The pattern is code being committed, built, packed, or signed by an account or on a host that does not normally perform that work, particularly when security, credential access, or persistence related code is involved and the artifact skips the normal review and release path. The fields that must be correlated are the author or triggering account, the repository and branch, the file names changed, the build artifact hash, the signing certificate, and the deployment target. The malicious case is an account with no development history committing an unsigned binary that later appears on production endpoints outside any change record. The benign case is a normal developer committing to a feature branch that is reviewed and released through the standard pipeline.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Suspicious Code Build or Signing Outside the Release Pipeline
# logsource:
#   product: linux
#   service: build
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action:
#       - 'build.start'
#       - 'artifact.sign'
#   filter_pipeline:
#     pipeline_id|contains: 'release-'
#     account|endswith: '-ci'
#   condition: selection and not filter_pipeline
# level: high
falsePositives: Security researchers building proof of concept tooling in an isolated laboratory environment
Developers compiling small helper utilities on their workstation for internal automation
Release engineering teams signing beta artifacts through a manual approval path during a hotfix
tuningNotes: Baseline which accounts, hosts and build definitions normally produce binaries, then filter the continuous integration service accounts and the standard release pipeline inside the rule and keep a separate review queue for exceptions. Scope the alert to repositories that produce deployable artifacts and to hosts outside the engineering network, and raise priority when a new binary reaches production endpoints without a matching change record. The coverage you lose is in house development that happens entirely on personal equipment outside management, so rely on network and cloud telemetry for the test infrastructure side.
